items.title: This architectural deep dive is currently in active development as part of the 8-part Enterprise Integration Patterns series on wiki.eiakoji.me. The formal theoretical derivations, Excalidraw-style schematics, Little's Law/queueing equations, and production Java 21 reference implementations will land directly in this publication entry.

children.text: In this installment, we formalize the following core integration patterns established by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, mapping each to its modern cloud-native realization:
End-to-End Enterprise Architecture: Composing all 65 EIP patterns into a production topology: Ingress Gateway, Fraud Scoring, Payment Processing, Inventory Allocation, and Logistics.
Macro-Topology Composition: Orchestrating high-throughput pipelines connecting transactional relational stores, distributed event logs, object storage, and legacy backbones.
Hybrid Orchestration & Choreography: Combining centralized Process Managers for long-running transactional sagas with decentralized pub-sub choreography for downstream analytics.
Cascading Backpressure Simulation: Simulating downstream database latency spikes and observing queue buffering, Little's Law dynamics, and consumer saturation.
Split-Brain Routing & Deadlock Resolution: Resolving conflicting concurrent updates and distributed state bifurcation across multi-region broker meshes.
Partial Failure Compensation: Executing backward compensation transactions across heterogeneous services when unrecoverable validation failures occur mid-workflow.
Engineering resilient enterprise integration topologies requires analyzing the exact failure boundaries and physical constraints governing these patterns:

System Synthesis Invariants: Individual pattern correctness does not guarantee macro-system stability; emergence in complex topologies introduces feedback loops, message amplification, and cascading backpressure.

Backpressure Propagation: Unbounded queues merely shift out-of-memory crashes from consumers to brokers; robust architectures enforce bounded queue capacities with explicit rate limiting at edge ingress.
Compensation Non-Atomicity: Distributed sagas rely on compensating transactions that may themselves fail; resilient systems require idempotent replay queues and automated reconciliation audits.
